LESSON 1 • Chronology & Geographical Causation

Mountains, Islands & Rival Poleis — Why Was Ancient Greece Divided Into City-States? (c. 800–500 BC)

Key Enquiry: Why did geography divide Ancient Greece into rival city-states, and what shared culture still united all Greeks?
[1.1] c. 2000–500 BC: Minoans, Mycenaeans & Mountain-Divided Poleis

Before marble temples rose in Athens, two Bronze Age peoples thrived around Greece. On Crete, Minoan sailors built painted palaces and traded across blue waves. Later, mainland Mycenaean kings raised giant stone fortresses guarded by the carved Lion Gate. Yet rugged land stopped Greece from uniting into one single kingdom.

Steep mountains sliced the mainland into narrow valleys, while over a thousand islands dotted the Aegean Sea. Travelling overland took days on rocky mule tracks, so communities grew up fiercely independent. Greeks built separate city-states called poleis, including Athens, Sparta, Corinth, and Thebes. Every polis guarded its own laws, citizen army, and silver coins.

[1.2] High City & Busy Market: Inside the Acropolis and the Agora

Although rival city-states often quarrelled, almost every Greek polis shared two famous town spaces. High above the rooftops stood a steep fortified hill called the Acropolis, meaning high city. Families climbed behind its thick stone walls whenever enemy soldiers marched near their farms. Citizens also crowned that hilltop with shining temples for their city's favourite protective god.

Down on flatter ground lay the Agora, a sunny open marketplace buzzing with voices. Farmers sold figs, goat cheese, and fresh fish while potters stacked painted clay bowls. Men also gathered there each morning to swap news and debate fair city laws.

[1.3] c. 800–500 BC: One Hellene Family, 24 Letters & Sea Trade

Across those divided valleys and islands, proud Greeks still called themselves Hellenes of one family. Everywhere they sailed, Greeks spoke one shared language and worshipped the same Olympian gods. Around 800 BC, merchants adapted Phoenician letters to invent a clever twenty-four-letter Greek alphabet. Adding vowel letters let writers carve clear stone laws and label painted pottery cups!

Because rocky hillsides had thin soil, farmers grew hardy olives and grapes instead of wide wheatfields. Wooden ships carried jars of golden olive oil and fine pottery across the Mediterranean Sea. Busy sea trade linked Greek harbours together while bringing home vital grain from overseas.

LESSON 2 • Similarity, Difference & Civic Comparison

Athens vs Sparta — Where Would You Rather Grow Up in Ancient Greece? (c. 508–430 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did democratic Athens and warrior Sparta govern their cities differently, and whose lives were freer in each polis?
[2.1] c. 508–430 BC: People-Power on the Pnyx & Who Was Left Out

Around 508 BC, citizens in sea-trading Athens invented a bold new government called demokratia, meaning people-power! Instead of obeying kings, adult male citizens climbed the rocky Pnyx hill every few days. Thousands debated war, taxes, and building plans before raising hands to vote directly on every law. Voters even scratched bossy leaders' names onto broken pottery ostrakon shards to banish them for ten years.

To stop rich people bribing courts, Athens slotted citizens' tickets into a marble kleroterion machine. Dropping coloured balls picked five hundred jurors fairly by chance! Yet Athenian direct democracy shut most residents out: women, enslaved people, and foreign-born metics could never vote.

[2.2] Two Kings & Tough Barracks: Growing Up Inside Warrior Sparta

Far inland beneath snowy Mount Taygetos lay Athens's toughest rival, land-locked Sparta. Spartans cared little for fancy speeches, silver coins, or marble theatres, prizing discipline and obedience instead. Two kings led Sparta's army alongside a strict council of older nobles. Conquered local farmworkers called helots toiled in the fields so Spartan citizens trained full-time for war.

At just seven years old, Spartan boys left home to enter harsh army barracks called the agoge. Barefoot in winter, they slept on scratchy river reeds, endured tough drills, and ate plain dark broth! Hungry boys were even dared to sneak extra food without getting caught.

[2.3] Boys, Girls & Women: Comparing Daily Life in Athens and Sparta

Growing up felt wildly different depending on whether you were born in Athens or Sparta! Wealthy Athenian boys paid tutors to teach reading, geometry, poetry, music, and graceful athletics. Athenian girls, however, rarely attended school, learning spinning, weaving, and household skills indoors under strict male guardians.

In Sparta, girls trained outdoors alongside boys at running, wrestling, and throwing the javelin! Because Spartan husbands spent years away in army barracks, Spartan women ran farms and owned land themselves. Visitors from Athens gasped to hear confident Spartan women speaking openly in public! Spartans believed strong, athletic mothers raised the bravest soldiers.

LESSON 3 • Beliefs, Culture & Source Evidence

Mount Olympus, Myths & The Ancient Olympics — How Did Religion Shape Greek Life? (776–400 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did belief in the Olympian gods inspire Greek temples, hero myths, and the Ancient Olympic Games?
[3.1] Twelve Gods on Snowy Mount Olympus & Gleaming Marble Temples

Religion wove through every single day in Ancient Greece! Greeks believed twelve immortal gods ruled from snowy Mount Olympus, Greece's tallest peak. Zeus hurled thunderbolts beside queen Hera, while Poseidon shook the seas and wise Athena guarded craftworkers and Athens. Twin gods Apollo and Artemis loved music and hunting, and winged-sandalled Hermes carried swift messages.

Cities built gleaming marble homes for their gods, such as Athens's Parthenon. Inside its inner hall stood a giant gold-and-ivory statue of Athena. Ordinary people worshipped outdoors at stone altars, pouring wine and roasting meat so fragrant smoke drifted skyward! Families also kept small home altars to thank the gods daily.

[3.2] Riddles at Mountain Delphi & Hero Myths on Painted Clay Vases

Before risking wars or sea voyages, anxious leaders climbed mountain Delphi to consult Apollo's Oracle. There, a priestess called the Pythia spoke mysterious riddles believed to come straight from Apollo! Generals puzzled over every word before marching armies or launching ships. Storytellers also chanted epic myths about brave heroes and terrifying monsters.

Families loved hearing how strong Heracles battled the many-headed Hydra, clever Odysseus outwitted giants, and Perseus faced snake-haired Medusa. Potters painted those thrilling adventures onto glossy black-figure and red-figure clay vases that still survive today! Painted jars turned Greek supper tables into lively storybooks of courage.

[3.3] 776 BC at Olympia: The Sacred Truce, Chariots & Olive Crowns

Religion even inspired the world's most famous sports festival! Every four summers from 776 BC, Greeks gathered at Olympia to honour Zeus with the Ancient Olympic Games. Before athletes set off, messengers proclaimed a Sacred Truce called Ekecheiria, pausing wars so rivals travelled safely. Athletes swore beside Zeus's smoky altar never to cheat in competition.

Crowds cheered the barefoot stadion sprint, discus, javelin, wrestling, and thunderous chariot racing! Winners received no gold medals, wearing a woven wild-olive crown called a kotinos that brought glory to their home polis. Hometown crowds welcomed champions back like heroes with songs and feasts!

LESSON 4 • Cause, Consequence & Turning Points

Marathon, Thermopylae & Salamis — How Did Tiny City-States Defeat the Persian Empire? (490–479 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did tiny, rival Greek city-states unite to defeat the mighty Persian Empire between 490 and 479 BC?
[4.1] 490 BC: Darius Invades, the Hoplite Phalanx & Marathon

Across the Aegean Sea lay the gigantic Achaemenid Persian Empire, ruled by King Darius I. In 490 BC, Darius sent warships to punish Athens for helping rebel Greek towns. Persian archers landed on the coastal plain of Marathon, north of Athens. Citizen hoplites marched out with bronze shields and long spears locked in a tight phalanx.

Charging at a run, the Greek phalanx smashed through the lighter Persian ranks and won! Legend tells how messenger Pheidippides raced twenty-six miles to Athens, shouted "Joy, we win!", and collapsed. His famous run inspired our modern marathon race, while Athenians heaped a grassy burial mound over their fallen heroes.

[4.2] 480 BC: King Xerxes & the Brave Stand at Thermopylae

Ten years later, in 480 BC, Darius’s son King Xerxes led an even bigger invasion. Vast armies including elite Persian Immortals marched south to conquer every free Greek city-state. Rival poleis united at last, sending Spartan King Leonidas to guard the narrow mountain pass of Thermopylae.

Steep cliffs towered on one side while deep sea waves crashed right below the road. For three fierce days, three hundred Spartans and brave Greek allies held back thousands of invaders. When a traitor showed Xerxes a hidden mountain path, Leonidas stayed fighting so allied troops could escape. Today a stone lion monument still honours their fearless courage.

[4.3] 480–479 BC: Wooden Triremes & Victory in the Strait of Salamis

Persian troops marched on and burned empty Athens, after Athenian families evacuated safely by boat. Clever Admiral Themistocles trusted Athens’s sleek wooden warships, called triremes, rowed by 170 oarsmen on three levels. Each fast trireme bore painted eyes on its prow and a heavy bronze ram at the waterline.

Themistocles sent a trick message that lured Xerxes’s huge fleet into the narrow Strait of Salamis. Jammed tightly together, giant Persian vessels collided while nimble Greek triremes rammed their wooden hulls. After Salamis in 480 BC and Plataea in 479 BC, Greece stayed independent and free!

LESSON 5 • Significance & History of Ideas

Theatre, Philosophy, Maths & Medicine — How Did Greek Thinkers Change Human Knowledge? (c. 460–322 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did Ancient Greek playwrights, philosophers, doctors, and mathematicians transform human knowledge?
[5.1] c. 460–330 BC: Hillside Amphitheatres, Masks, Tragedies & Comedies

After defeating Persia, Greek city-states entered a golden age of drama, science, and bold ideas. Builders carved semicircular stone amphitheatres into sunny hillsides, such as Epidaurus, seating 14,000 spectators. Clever curved stone acoustics carried even a quiet whisper from the round stage to the back row!

During festivals for Dionysus, male actors staged serious tragedies about pride and funny comedies teasing leaders. Performers wore painted clay or linen theatre masks with wide mouths so distant crowds saw clear faces. Poorer citizens even received state coins so everyone could attend. Watching plays together taught Greek citizens to debate fairness, courage, and tough moral choices.

[5.2] c. 430–322 BC: Athens’s Philosophers — Socrates, Plato & Aristotle

In busy Athens, bold thinkers called philosophers, meaning "lovers of wisdom", asked how people should live. Barefoot Socrates walked around the Agora asking sharp questions that made citizens test their own beliefs. In 399 BC, angry jurors condemned Socrates, yet he bravely drank poison rather than stop questioning.

His devoted pupil Plato founded a shady garden school in Athens called the Academy to share wisdom. Plato’s brightest student, Aristotle, studied nature closely by observing, measuring, and sorting real facts. Aristotle classified hundreds of plants and animals, laying vital foundations for modern science and logic. Later, Aristotle opened his own shady school called the Lyceum.

[5.3] c. 420–212 BC: Hippocrates on Kos, Geometry & Archimedes’s "Eureka!"

For centuries, sick people blamed illnesses on angry gods and begged priests for magic cures. On the island of Kos, doctor Hippocrates taught physicians to observe symptoms, clean diet, fresh air, and rest. Modern doctors still promise to care ethically for patients, honouring his famous Hippocratic Oath.

Greek mathematicians also unlocked rules of numbers, shapes, and machines that engineers still use today. Pythagoras studied right-angled triangles, while Euclid wrote a clear geometry guide to lines and angles. Later, Archimedes mastered levers and reportedly leaped from his bath shouting "Eureka!" after solving a puzzle!

LESSON 6 • Change, Continuity & Lasting Legacy

Alexander the Great & Our World Today — What Is Ancient Greece’s Lasting Legacy? (336–146 BC & Today)

Key Enquiry: How did Alexander the Great spread Greek culture, and what is Ancient Greece’s lasting legacy in our world today?
[6.1] 336–323 BC: Young King Alexander, Bucephalus & a Vast Empire

North of the old poleis lay mountainous Macedon, where young prince Alexander was tutored by Aristotle. As a boy, Alexander tamed a wild black warhorse named Bucephalus by turning him toward the sun. Crowned king in 336 BC aged twenty, Alexander the Great united Greece and marched east against Persia.

Over eleven years, Alexander never lost a battle, leading troops across Egypt, Persia, and north-west India. Before dying aged thirty-two in 323 BC, he founded dozens of cities named Alexandria. Blending Greek speech and art with Egyptian and Asian customs created the lively Hellenistic world. Traders, artists, and scholars now travelled freely from Greece to Asia.

[6.2] 323–146 BC: Alexandria’s Great Library, Pharos & Conquering Rome

Egypt’s port of Alexandria became a wonder of learning, lit by its towering Pharos Lighthouse. Inside the Great Library, scholars gathered hundreds of thousands of papyrus scrolls on stars, maps, and geometry. Thinkers from distant lands studied Euclid’s diagrams and shared discoveries in a common Greek language.

Meanwhile, a mighty new power rose west across the sea in Italy: the Roman Republic. In 146 BC, tough Roman legions conquered mainland Greece and ruled its old city-states. Yet Romans deeply admired Greek culture, copying marble statues, hiring Greek teachers, and matching Roman gods to Olympians. Educated Romans proudly read Homer’s poems and learned to speak Greek.

[6.3] 1896 & Today: Democracy, Words, Columns & the Modern Olympics

Over two thousand years have passed since ancient Greece flourished. Yet its rich legacy still shapes Britain and the wider world. Whenever citizens vote in elections or serve on courtroom juries, they echo Athenian democracy. Hundreds of common English words come from Greek, including school, dinosaur, planet, music, theatre, and history!

Look up at grand museums or town halls to spot Doric, Ionic, and leafy Corinthian stone columns. In 1896, athletes met inside Athens’s marble Panathenaic Stadium to launch the Modern Olympic Games. From geometry lessons to Olympic medals, Greek curiosity still inspires our world every single day!

Whole-Unit Knowledge Check (Lessons 1–6)

Please do not write inside this reusable textbook — answer orally with your partner or in your exercise book!

Lesson 1: Mountains, Islands & Rival Poleis
  1. Which famous gateway guarded the Bronze Age mainland fortress of Mycenae around 1250 BC?
  2. Why did Ancient Greece develop into separate city-states (poleis) instead of one united kingdom?
  3. Inside a Greek polis, what was the difference between the Acropolis and the Agora?
  4. From which seafaring traders did Greeks adapt symbols around 800 BC to create their 24-letter alphabet?
  5. Which two symbols did Athens proudly stamp onto its silver tetradrachm coins?
Lesson 2: Athens vs Sparta
  1. What does the Ancient Greek word 'demokratia' (invented in Athens around 508 BC) literally mean?
  2. Which groups living in Athens were completely shut out from voting on the Pnyx hill?
  3. What job did the slotted marble 'kleroterion' machine do in Athens?
  4. At what age did Spartan citizen boys leave home to enter the tough 'agoge' military barracks?
  5. How did Spartan women's lives surprise visitors from democratic Athens?
Lesson 3: Mount Olympus, Myths & The Ancient Olympics
  1. Where did Ancient Greeks believe the twelve chief Olympian gods and goddesses lived?
  2. Which gleaming marble temple was built atop Athens's Acropolis to honour wise warrior goddess Athena?
  3. Why did Greek kings, generals, and travellers climb high up to the sanctuary of Delphi?
  4. In what year were the first recorded Ancient Olympic Games held at Olympia in honour of Zeus?
  5. What did the 'Sacred Truce' (Ekecheiria) do before every Ancient Olympic Games, and what prize did winners receive?
Lesson 4: Marathon, Thermopylae & Salamis
  1. What do historians call the tight shoulder-to-shoulder battle formation of Greek hoplites locking shields together?
  2. Which legendary messenger ran roughly twenty-six miles from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens in 490 BC?
  3. Which Spartan king led 300 Spartans and Greek allies to hold the narrow mountain pass of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
  4. How many oarsmen rowed an ancient Greek wooden trireme, and what weapon sat at its waterline prow?
  5. Which Athenian commander lured King Xerxes’s huge fleet into a trap inside the narrow Strait of Salamis in 480 BC?
Lesson 5: Theatre, Philosophy, Maths & Medicine
  1. Roughly how many spectators could sit inside the curved stone hillside amphitheatre at Epidaurus and still hear clearly?
  2. What were the two main types of plays performed by masked actors at Greek festivals for Dionysus?
  3. What does the Greek word "philosopher" literally mean, and which three thinkers formed Athens’s famous chain of teachers?
  4. On the island of Kos, how did physician Hippocrates change the way Greek doctors treated sick patients?
  5. Which Greek thinker famously shouted "Eureka!" ("I have found it!") and explained how levers lift heavy loads?
Lesson 6: Alexander the Great & Our World Today
  1. Which famous philosopher tutored young Alexander of Macedon, and what was the name of Alexander’s beloved warhorse?
  2. Which two famous landmarks stood in Egypt’s Hellenistic city of Alexandria?
  3. What happened in 146 BC when the Roman Republic conquered mainland Greece?
  4. How can you recognise a Greek Corinthian column capital compared with plain Doric and scrolled Ionic capitals?
  5. Where and when were the first Modern Olympic Games revived, and which of these everyday English words come from Greek?

KEY STAGE 2 ILLUSTRATED GLOSSARY SYLLABLE HELPERS & DEFINITIONS

Historian's Word Bank (24 Essential Terms)

Clap the italic syllables out loud together to master new historical words with confidence!

Polis Po-lis
An independent Ancient Greek city-state — including the walled town and surrounding farmland — that made its own laws (plural: poleis).
Acropolis A-crop-o-lis
The high rocky fortified hilltop at the centre of a Greek city-state, crowned with defensive walls and marble temples.
Agora Ag-o-ra
The bustling open-air marketplace and meeting square in a Greek city-state where people shopped, chatted, and debated laws.
Alphabet Al-pha-bet
The 24-letter Greek writing system with vowels and consonants, adapted from Phoenician sea traders around 800 BC.
Democracy De-moc-ra-cy
Rule by the people (from Greek demokratia = people-power), invented in Athens around 508 BC so male citizens voted directly on laws.
Ostrakon Os-tra-kon
A broken pottery shard scratched with a politician's name by Athenian voters to banish dangerous leaders from the city for ten years.
Kleroterion Kle-ro-te-ri-on
A slotted marble machine in Athens that used falling black and white balls to pick 500 courtroom jurors fairly by chance.
Metics Met-ics
Free foreign-born craftworkers and traders living permanently in Athens who paid taxes yet were barred from voting as citizens.
Mount Olympus Mount O-lym-pus
Greece's highest snow-capped mountain, where Ancient Greeks believed the twelve chief gods and goddesses lived above the clouds.
Parthenon Par-the-non
The magnificent white-marble temple built high on the Acropolis of Athens in the 400s BC to honour wise warrior goddess Athena.
Oracle Or-a-cle
A sacred shrine — most famously Apollo's mountain sanctuary at Delphi — where Greeks asked a priestess for wise advice from the gods.
Sacred Truce Sa-cred Truce
The peaceful agreement (Ekecheiria) announced before every Ancient Olympic Games so warring city-states paused fighting for safe travel.
Empire Em-pire
Many different lands and peoples ruled together by one powerful king or emperor, such as Achaemenid Persia.
Hoplite Hop-lite
A heavily armed Greek citizen-soldier carrying a round bronze-faced shield, crested helmet, and long thrusting spear.
Phalanx Pha-lanx
A tight shoulder-to-shoulder battle block of Greek hoplites locking shields together behind a forest of spears.
Trireme Tri-reme
A fast ancient Greek wooden warship powered by 170 oarsmen on three levels and armed with a bronze ram.
Amphitheatre Am-phi-the-a-tre
An open-air stone theatre with rising semicircular tiers of seats carved into a Greek hillside, such as Epidaurus.
Tragedy Trag-e-dy
A serious Greek play exploring sorrow, pride, fate, and difficult moral choices made by heroes or rulers.
Comedy Com-e-dy
A lively, funny Greek play packed with jokes, costumes, and clever teasing of famous leaders or everyday habits.
Philosopher Phi-los-o-pher
From Greek words meaning "lover of wisdom": a thinker like Socrates, Plato, or Aristotle who searches for truth.
Macedon Mac-e-don
The rugged northern Greek kingdom ruled by Alexander the Great, who united Greece in 336 BC.
Hellenistic Hel-len-is-tic
The vibrant blended culture created when Alexander’s conquests mixed Greek language and art with Egyptian and Asian ideas.
Alexandria Al-ex-an-dri-a
Famous Egyptian port city founded by Alexander, home to the Pharos Lighthouse and the ancient world’s greatest library.
Column Col-umn
An upright stone pillar holding up a roof, carved by Greeks in plain Doric, scrolled Ionic, or leafy Corinthian styles.

MASTER CHRONOLOGICAL SPINE c. 800 BC TO 146 BC

10 Turning Points Across Ancient Greece

c. 1600–1200 BC
Minoans & Mycenaeans: Bronze Age Knossos on Crete and Mycenaean citadels inspire myths of the Labyrinth and Troy.
c. 800 BC
City-States & Vowel Alphabet: Independent poleis grow between mountains and sea; Greeks add vowels and write Homer’s epics.
776 BC
First Olympic Games & Truce: Rival city-states pause wars every four years to honour Zeus and compete for olive wreaths.
508 BC
Athenian Direct Democracy: Cleisthenes launches citizen Assembly voting on the Pnyx hill (contrasting with two-king Sparta).
490 BC
Victory at Marathon: Heavily armoured Greek hoplites charge in phalanx formation to defeat Darius’s Persian landing.
480 BC
Thermopylae & Salamis: Leonidas holds Thermopylae’s pass before Themistocles’ wooden triremes win at Salamis.
447–432 BC
The Marble Parthenon: Pericles and Phidias crown the Acropolis with Classical Doric and Ionic marble architecture.
c. 430–350 BC
Theatre, Philosophy & Medicine: Masked drama, Socrates/Plato/Aristotle, and Hippocrates’ clinical medicine flourish.
336–146 BC
Alexander & Hellenistic Science: Alexander spreads Greek cities to Egypt and India; Alexandria’s Library advances geometry until Rome rules (146 BC).
AD 1896–Today
Modern Olympics & Living Legacy: Modern Olympics revive in Athens while democracy, juries, and Greek words shape our world.
Big Picture Historian Discussion

1. Fair Comparison: How was modern British democracy inspired by Ancient Athens—and how is modern voting much fairer today?
2. Ideas Stronger Than Armies: Even though Roman legions conquered Greece in 146 BC, why do historians say Greek culture captivated Rome?
